name: Design a Configuration Management Service
intent: Change settings for tens of thousands of running services without redeploying them, roll the change out in stages, and make a bad value easy to undo and impossible to turn into an outage of the whole fleet.
codeTitle: versioned config with staged rollout and a last-known-good cache
finalIntro: One timeout change moving through review, validation, a staged rollout and a restart during an outage.
prompt: Design a configuration service for a company with 2,000 services running on 50,000 instances in several environments. Teams change settings such as timeouts, limits and feature switches. A change should reach production within minutes, be validated before it goes out, be rolled out gradually, be undone quickly, and never stop the services from starting.
functional: Store configuration as versions, and read the current version of a service's configuration
Validate a change against a schema before it is accepted
Roll a change out to a growing share of instances, and roll it back
Deliver changes to running instances by polling or by push
Layer per-environment, per-region and per-service overrides on a shared base
Keep an audit trail of who changed what and when, with approvals
nonFunctional: A change reaches every instance within about a minute after its rollout is released
Services keep working and can restart while the config service is down
The config service handles tens of thousands of instances polling at once, cheaply
A bad value must be stopped by validation, or limited by the rollout to a few percent of instances
Rollback takes effect within one polling interval
Every change is attributed, reviewed and can be reproduced later

firstAttempt.text: Config files live in each service's repository and are baked into the build, or set as environment variables by the deploy script. To change a timeout, a developer edits the file, merges it and redeploys the service. Production, staging and development have their own copies of the file.
limits: Every config change needs a full build and deploy, so a simple fix takes an hour instead of a minute
The change reaches all instances at once, so one typo is an outage of the whole service
Nothing checks the value: a timeout of 0 or the text 'fast' is only found when the process starts or fails
Rolling back means another full deploy, and nobody can say which value was live at a given time
Copies per environment drift apart, and a secret in a file ends up in the repository

steps.title: Serve versioned configuration from a central store
steps.problem: Configuration that is baked into builds can only change with a deploy, and nobody can say which value was live when.
steps.fix: Move configuration into a store where every change creates a new immutable version with an author, a time and a checksum. Instances ask a small config API for the current version of their configuration, sending the version they already have. If nothing changed the API answers 'not modified' without a body. Because a version never changes after it is written, the response can be cached by a CDN or a proxy, and going back to an earlier value just means pointing the 'stable' marker at an older version.
steps.tradeoff: Changes take effect in minutes without a build, and history comes for free. The config service becomes a dependency of every service, so it must be very reliable and must never be needed at the moment a service is starting.

steps.title: Validate every change before it can go live
steps.problem: A value of the wrong type, a negative timeout or a missing key is not noticed until a process fails, and the failure then happens on every instance at once.
steps.fix: Every key has a schema that gives its type, its allowed range and its default, and the service refuses to save a version that breaks it. Cross-field rules catch more, for example the retry budget must fit inside the timeout. Changes go through review, and the editor sees a diff against the live version and a dry-run result. The same schema is shipped to the client library, which checks again before it applies anything. Adding a key or widening a range must stay compatible with older clients that are still running.
steps.tradeoff: Typos and impossible values never reach production. A schema cannot know that a valid value is a bad choice, such as a 60 ms timeout on a slow dependency, so validation is the first layer and the rollout is the second.

steps.title: Roll out in stages with a health gate and an instant rollback
steps.problem: A valid but harmful change reaches every instance within one polling interval, and a person has to notice it and react.
steps.fix: A rollout controller releases a version to a growing share of instances: for example 1%, 5%, 25% and then 100%, with a bake time at each stage. Which instances are in a stage is decided by a stable hash of the instance id, so the same instances stay in the early group, and the first groups can be a canary region or low-risk services. Between stages the controller compares the error rate, latency and restarts of the new group with the old group. If the gate fails, it moves the candidate share back to 0%, and the instances return to the stable version at their next poll.
steps.tradeoff: A bad change hurts a few percent of the fleet for a minute or two instead of everything for half an hour. A full rollout is slower by the sum of the bake times, so urgent fixes need a fast path that is audited, and a gate is only as good as the metrics it watches.

steps.title: Poll with a push hint, and keep a last-known-good copy
steps.problem: Instances need new values quickly, but 50,000 instances should not hammer the config service, and a service must still start when the config service is down.
steps.fix: Instances poll every 30 seconds with a random offset, sending the version they hold, so almost every answer is a tiny 'not modified'. A change notifier adds a hint over a long-lived connection ('version 43 exists') so urgent changes arrive in a second or two, but the poll stays as the safety net when a hint is lost. A new version is verified by checksum and schema, written to local disk and only then applied. The library marks it last-known-good after the instance has been healthy for a while. At start-up the instance reads that file first, so it runs without the config service, and keeps retrying with backoff and jitter in the background.
steps.tradeoff: The config service is not on the critical path of a running service, and its load is a steady, cacheable trickle. Instances can run on slightly old values for a while during an outage, so a value that must change everywhere at the same instant is not a good fit.

steps.title: Layer overrides for each environment, region and service
steps.problem: Production, staging and each region differ in a few values, and separate full copies drift apart.
steps.fix: Keep one base configuration and add small override layers that apply in a fixed order: base, then environment, then region, then cluster, then a single service or instance, where the most specific layer wins. The service computes the merged result for each instance when it is requested, and the version of the merged result is derived from the versions of the layers that went into it. Each layer has its own owner and its own permissions, and the diff shows exactly which layer set a value. Overrides go through the same schema and rollout as any other change.
steps.tradeoff: Environments differ only where they are meant to, and a new region starts from the base. Too many layers make it hard to see why an instance has a value, so the service must offer an 'explain this value' view and a limit on how deep the layers go.

steps.title: Audit every change, control who can make it, and keep secrets out
steps.problem: When something breaks, the first question is what changed. An answer of 'someone edited a file' is not enough, and config files have a habit of collecting passwords.
steps.fix: Every version, rollout stage, rollback and permission change is written to an append-only audit log with the actor, the diff, the approver and the reason. Permissions are per key and per environment, and production needs a second person to approve. Secrets are never stored as values: a key holds a reference such as 'secret:payments/db', and the instance resolves it at runtime from the secrets manager. The log is exported to dashboards, so a graph can show a marker at every config change and an incident can be traced back to the exact version.
steps.tradeoff: Incidents are easier to explain, and the blast radius of a stolen account is limited. Approvals slow down changes, so low-risk keys can be marked as self-service, and reading secrets at run time adds one more dependency.

failures.scenario: A change passes the schema but breaks the service
failures.impact: A timeout of 60 ms is a valid integer, but every call to a slow dependency now fails.
failures.answer: The rollout is staged, so only the first 5% of instances saw it. The gate compared error rates, saw the new group fail, and moved the candidate share back to 0%. Those instances went back to the stable version at their next poll, and the audit log shows the exact change for the follow-up.

failures.scenario: The config service is down while instances restart
failures.impact: If a service must fetch its configuration to start, a config outage turns into a restart that cannot finish, for every service at once.
failures.answer: Each instance starts from its last-known-good file on local disk, and the image carries safe defaults for a brand-new instance. Fetching happens in the background with backoff and jitter. The loss is that no changes are delivered while the service is down, which is acceptable.

failures.scenario: All 50,000 instances poll the instant the service comes back
failures.impact: The first healthy second brings a wall of requests, the service falls over again, and the cycle repeats.
failures.answer: Polling uses a random offset and exponential backoff with jitter, so retries spread out. Conditional requests make most answers tiny, a CDN or regional proxy absorbs identical responses, and the API sheds load when it is overloaded instead of queueing it.

failures.scenario: A push hint is lost or an instance misses a version
failures.impact: Some instances stay on an old value, and a half-applied rollout looks healthy.
failures.answer: The hint is only a shortcut. The next poll compares versions and fetches what is missing, and the controller reports how many instances are on each version, so a laggard is visible. The checksum also catches a damaged download, which is discarded in favour of the cached copy.

failures.scenario: Two engineers edit the same key at once
failures.impact: The second save silently overwrites the first, and a change vanishes without anyone noticing.
failures.answer: A save names the version it was based on. If the live version has moved on, the store rejects it with a conflict, and the editor shows a merge of both changes to review again.

alternatives.title: How changes reach instances

options.name: Polling with conditional requests
options.pro: Simple, robust and cacheable, and the load is steady and predictable
options.con: A change takes up to one interval to arrive

options.name: Push over a persistent connection
options.pro: Changes arrive in about a second
options.con: Needs a connection per instance, reconnect handling and a fallback when a message is lost

options.name: Poll plus a push hint
options.pro: Fast in the normal case, and correct even when the hint is lost

alternatives.pick: Poll as the base and add a push hint when seconds matter.

alternatives.title: Where the configuration is stored

options.name: Files in a Git repository
options.pro: Review, diff and history already exist
options.con: Not built for fast reads at scale, so it needs a service in front and a way to promote changes

options.name: A key-value store with consensus
options.pro: Strongly consistent reads and watches, such as etcd or ZooKeeper
options.con: Poor fit for tens of thousands of clients and for large documents

options.name: A database with a read-through cache
options.con: Needs care so the cache never shows two clients different data for long

alternatives.pick: Git or a database as the source of truth, served through a stateless, cacheable API.

alternatives.title: Config at build time or at run time

options.name: Baked into the build
options.pro: Reproducible and always available at start-up

options.name: Fetched at run time
options.pro: Changes in minutes, with no deploy
options.con: A dependency, and a change can break a running service

alternatives.pick: Run time for settings that change often, build time for structure, and local defaults and a cache for safety.

alternatives.title: How a rollout is targeted

options.name: Random percentage of instances
options.pro: Easy to reason about and statistically even
options.con: May hit the same service's whole critical path at once

options.name: By region, cluster or service tier
options.pro: Limits the blast radius to a known area
options.con: Early groups are not representative of the rest

alternatives.pick: Start with a low-risk region or tier, then a percentage within the rest.

roles.description: The read path that instances poll.

roles.label: Signals
roles.description: Change hints going out and health metrics coming back.

roles.label: State
roles.description: Versions, overrides, the local cache and the audit log.

quiz.question: A developer sets a request timeout to 60 ms for a slow dependency. The value is a valid integer, so the schema accepts it, and the config service releases it to all 50,000 instances at once. Within a minute every call to that dependency fails. Which addition best limits the damage of the next change like this?
options: A second reviewer who must approve every production change, so that two people have looked at each value before it ships to the fleet
A stricter schema with a minimum of 100 ms for every key that holds a timeout, checked again by the client library
A faster polling interval of 5 seconds, so that a corrected value reaches the instances sooner after a bad release
A staged rollout from 1% to 5% to 25% that compares the new group's errors with the old group's and reverts if the gate fails
quiz.explanation: A schema cannot know that a valid value is a bad choice, so the rollout is the second layer: only a few percent are hurt, and the gate sends them back. Reviewers and a fixed minimum miss the next odd case, and faster polling spreads the bad value faster.

quiz.question: 50,000 instances poll the config service every 30 seconds, and nearly every answer is a tiny 'not modified'. Urgent changes must now reach all instances within about 2 seconds. Assume the service can handle a steady 2,000 requests a second. Which approach fits?
options: Keep the 30 second poll and add a push hint saying a new version exists
Poll every 2 seconds, since answers are tiny and the service only needs a larger load balancer
Replace polling with push only over long-lived connections, and make instances wait for the connection to be restored before applying anything
Lower the config API's response cache time to zero so that each 30-second poll always sees the newest version of the configuration
quiz.explanation: The poll costs about 1,700 requests a second now, and a 2 second poll would need 25,000. The hint carries the news fast, and the poll is the safety net if a hint is lost. Push only has no fallback, and a cache change does not make instances ask more often.

quiz.question: The config service is down for 2 hours. During that time a deploy restarts 300 instances of one service, and each instance blocks at start-up until it has fetched its configuration, so none of them come up. What is the best change?
options: Retry the fetch with exponential backoff and jitter for up to 10 minutes before giving up, so the config service gets time to recover first
Run the config service in a second region, so that one region failing cannot stop an instance from fetching its configuration
Start from a verified last-known-good copy on local disk or safe image defaults, and fetch updates in the background with backoff
Keep the last version in process memory, so that the instance can use it while it is running
quiz.explanation: A starting service must never need the config service, so it takes the local copy and refreshes later. Longer retries and a second region still leave start-up dependent on the service, and a copy in memory is lost exactly when the process restarts.
